issues.description: In Experiment 1, the mixed model includes only a random intercept for subjects but no random intercept or slope for items (suffixes or nonwords). Given that stimuli vary systematically in their properties and multiple nonwords share the same suffix, failing to account for item-level variance risks inflated Type I error rates. This is a well-known issue in psycholinguistic research (Clark, 1973; Barr et al., 2013). The same concern applies to Experiment 2, which also only includes a random intercept for subjects.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent test statistics across text and table
issues.description: For the regressions-out measure in Experiment 3, the text reports B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01, but Table 5 reports B = 0.25, z = 2.65, p < 0.01. These values are inconsistent for what should be the same analysis. Either the text or the table contains an error.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01).

issues.description: For go-past time, the text reports B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001, but Table 5 reports B = 43, t = 3.76, p < 0.001. Additionally, the raw mean difference in Table 5 is 49 ms (507-458), which doesn't match either estimate closely. These inconsistencies suggest possible errors in reporting or different model specifications.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.description: No power analyses or sample size justifications are provided for any of the three experiments (N=46, N=29, N=47). Without these, it is impossible to evaluate whether the studies were adequately powered to detect the effects of interest, particularly for the graded diagnosticity/specificity analyses which involve continuous moderators.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory directional predictions for diagnosticity vs. specificity
issues.description: The authors predict that diagnosticity (spelling-to-meaning) should impact tasks requiring access to grammatical information from print (Experiments 1 and 3), while specificity (meaning-to-spelling) should impact spelling production (Experiment 2). However, they label this as 'feedforward' effects, which is confusing because diagnosticity describes the forward mapping from spelling to meaning, yet they also state 'we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning.' This appears to reverse the predicted direction: diagnosticity should logically affect reading (print-to-meaning), not spelling production, and specificity should affect spelling (meaning-to-print), not reading. The actual experiments seem to test the correct mapping (diagnosticity for reading/classification, specificity for spelling), contradicting this stated prediction.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the number of words before the target differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs. 5.23, p < 0.05). This means the amount of preceding context differs across conditions, which could affect expectations and processing difficulty independently of the congruency manipulation. The authors acknowledge this but do not address its potential impact on results.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.subcategory: Comprehension accuracy reported as percentage not proportion
issues.description: Average comprehension accuracy is reported as 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%), which appears to be a typographical error—these should be proportions (0.86) or percentages (86%). As written, 0.86% accuracy would indicate near-chance performance, suggesting participants were not reading for comprehension.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: High missing data rate in Experiment 1
issues.description: 11.7% of data points were missing in Experiment 1 due to timeouts or non-responses. With 46 participants and 40 items each, this represents approximately 215 missing data points out of 1,840 expected. The authors do not analyze whether missingness was systematic (e.g., more timeouts for certain suffix types or conditions), which could bias results.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.subcategory: Inclusion of pseudoaffixed words conflates morphological and orthographic cues
issues.description: The computational analysis deliberately includes pseudoaffixed words (e.g., VANISH for -ISH) because 'there is evidence that people identify morphemes within these.' However, this conflates genuine morphological relationships with orthographic overlap. The diagnosticity and specificity measures are then presented as capturing morphological regularities, but they actually capture a mixture of morphological and orthographic patterns. This undermines the claim that the results specifically reflect morphological knowledge rather than sensitivity to orthographic regularities.
issues.quote: We included pseudoaffixed words because there is evidence that people identify morphemes within these (Rastle, Davis, & New, 2004).

issues.description: The authors acknowledge having no concrete predictions about which eye-movement measures would show effects, and chose to monitor a variety of measures. With six dependent variables tested, there is an elevated risk of Type I error due to multiple comparisons, and no correction for multiple testing is applied. The significant results on go-past time and regressions-out could reflect selective reporting from among many tested measures.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: Missing details on random effects structure in Experiment 3
issues.description: For Experiment 3, the authors state models included 'random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes' but do not report random slopes. Given the within-subject, within-item nature of the congruency manipulation, maximal random effects structures (including random slopes for congruency by subjects and by items) should be considered. The justification for the chosen structure is not provided.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes.

issues.description: In Experiment 2, each participant saw all 66 sentences, with each suffix appearing three times in congruent and three times in incongruent contexts. There is no counterbalancing of which specific nonwords appear in which condition across participants. This means that any idiosyncratic properties of specific nonwords are confounded with condition for particular suffixes.
issues.quote: Each subject saw all 66 sentences.

issues.description: All three experiments used undergraduate students from a single university (Royal Holloway, University of London). The authors claim results reflect properties of 'skilled readers' and 'the average reader' but do not acknowledge limitations of this restricted sample in terms of age, education level, socioeconomic background, or reading experience.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent token analysis reporting in Experiment 2
issues.description: For the token-based specificity analysis in Experiment 2, the authors report 'z = 0.60, p < 0.01' for the interaction. A z-value of 0.60 would correspond to p ≈ 0.55, not p < 0.01. This is either a reporting error in the z-value or the p-value.
issues.quote: As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: Confound between suffix and lexical category in Experiment 1
issues.description: In Experiment 1, suffixes are inherently confounded with lexical category—noun suffixes differ from adjective suffixes in many ways beyond diagnosticity (length, frequency, phonological properties, orthographic familiarity). While the graded diagnosticity analysis partially addresses this, the basic condition effect (noun vs. adjective suffix) cannot be unambiguously attributed to diagnosticity knowledge rather than other correlated properties of the suffixes.
issues.quote: Using our linguistic analysis, we selected suffixes that are diagnostic for adjectives or nouns, and created nonwords ending in these suffixes.

issues.description: The authors claim that the knowledge demonstrated in the experiments was 'acquired through implicit statistical learning processes' and that participants were 'never taught these relationships explicitly.' However, no evidence is provided to rule out explicit learning or metalinguistic awareness. The classification task in Experiment 1 explicitly asks about lexical categories, and participants may have explicit knowledge of suffix-category relationships from formal education.
issues.quote: It is unlikely that our participants were ever taught these relationships explicitly; more likely is that this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes

issues.description: The entropy analysis comparing Hspelling and Hsound yields a slope of 0.9, which is statistically different from 1. However, the practical difference between mean H values (0.61 vs. 0.63) is very small. The authors interpret this as evidence that 'spelling is more predictive of category compared to phonology,' but the effect size is minimal and may not be linguistically meaningful. The regression approach also assumes a linear relationship between spelling and phonological entropy, which may not be appropriate.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.description: No effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, odds ratios, R²) are reported for any of the three experiments. Only raw regression coefficients and test statistics are provided, making it difficult to evaluate the practical significance of the findings.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001)

issues.description: Experiment 1 was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session. Fatigue or carryover effects from the prior session could influence performance, particularly given the 2-second timeout and the 11.7% missing data rate. This is not discussed as a potential limitation.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.description: For several suffixes in Table 2 and Appendix A, the diagnosticity values across the three categories (A, N, V) do not sum to 1.0. For example, +fold has diagnosticity values of 0.414 (A) + 0.138 (N) + 0.103 (V) = 0.655, and +ly has 0.039 + 0.006 + 0.002 = 0.047. This suggests either additional categories are being used (e.g., adverbs) that are not accounted for, or there is an error in the computation. The authors state they consider only three categories (nouns, adjectives, verbs), but many suffixes appear in words of other categories (e.g., adverbs for -ly). This is not adequately explained.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

issues.subcategory: Diagnosticity measure conflates category-specificity with category frequency
issues.description: The diagnosticity measure (proportion of words with a suffix belonging to a given category) is influenced by the base rate of that category in the language. If nouns are more frequent than adjectives overall, a suffix appearing equally in both would have higher diagnosticity for nouns simply due to base rates. The measure does not account for the prior probability of each category, which could inflate diagnosticity values for the most common category.
issues.quote: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: The text states diagnosticity is calculated by 'dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.' This would compute P(suffix|category), not P(category|suffix). However, diagnosticity is conceptually described as 'the strength with which a suffix spelling predicts lexical category,' which is P(category|suffix). The formula described computes specificity-like values, not diagnosticity as conceptually defined. Later the text says 'Diagnosticity on its own is reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity (conditional probability of a category given a cue),' confirming the intended measure is P(category|suffix), but the formula given computes something different.
issues.quote: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the authors multiplied diagnosticity by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes to create a single continuous predictor. This transformation assumes a linear relationship and imposes a specific functional form on the data. The separate analyses for adjective and noun suffixes partially address this, but the initial combined analysis could be misleading if the relationship differs in form across the two suffix types.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: Missing information about list assignment in Experiment 1
issues.description: Stimuli were divided into two lists of 40 items, but the authors do not report how many participants were assigned to each list, whether assignment was random, or whether list was included as a factor in the analysis.
issues.quote: Stimuli were divided into two experimental lists with 40 items per list. Participants saw only one list; each suffix occurred twice only.

issues.subcategory: Verb fillers not analyzed in Experiment 3
issues.description: Forty filler nonwords with verb suffixes were included in Experiment 3 but not analyzed because 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category.' This means the congruency manipulation was only tested for nouns and adjectives, limiting the generalizability of the findings. Furthermore, participants saw verb contexts only as fillers, which could create response biases or expectations.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category

issues.subcategory: Missing details on convergence warning resolution
issues.description: The authors report a convergence warning for the regressions-out model and refit using a different optimizer (bobyqa). While they state the fits were identical, they do not report the actual parameter estimates from the original model to allow comparison, nor do they consider whether the convergence issue might indicate model misspecification rather than simply an optimizer problem.
issues.quote: The original model produced a convergence warning when the variables were added. One way to assess if this warning is a false positive is to refit this model using a different optimisation procedure, such as "bobyqa" (Powell, 2009).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants were explicitly told to classify nonwords as nouns or adjectives and given definitions of these categories. This explicit framing may have encouraged participants to use metalinguistic strategies rather than reflecting implicit knowledge of spelling-category regularities. The forced binary choice (noun vs. adjective) also prevents participants from indicating uncertainty or choosing other categories.
issues.quote: You will be asked to decide if a letter string looks like a noun or an adjective. NOUN is a person, animal, place, thing, or idea... ADJECTIVE is an attribute of a noun

issues.description: The authors state they excluded 64 suffixes occurring in fewer than 20 words, leaving 95 suffixes for analysis. However, 154 - 64 = 90, not 95. This arithmetic discrepancy is unexplained.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes

issues.description: The authors argue that spelling-sound inconsistency in English may be functional because it allows spellings to become reserved for meaningful functions. However, this argument is somewhat circular: the existence of multiple spellings for the same sound is both the phenomenon to be explained (spelling-sound inconsistency) and the proposed explanation (allowing spelling-meaning regularity). Without diachronic evidence that spelling-meaning regularity drove the development of spelling-sound inconsistency (rather than being a byproduct), this functional claim is speculative.
issues.quote: the proliferation of spellings in English may actually be functional... irregularity in the English spelling-sound mapping may permit regularity in the spelling-meaning mapping. This fractionation could not occur in a spelling-sound transparent writing system.

issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration for any of the three experiments. Given the multiple dependent variables in Experiment 3 and the exploratory nature of some analyses (e.g., the graded diagnosticity/specificity analyses), pre-registration would have been valuable for distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory findings.

issues.subcategory: Single speaker for auditory stimuli in Experiment 2
issues.description: All auditory stimuli in Experiment 2 were produced by a single speaker. Despite using IPA transcriptions, the speaker may have introduced subtle prosodic or phonetic cues that could influence spelling choices. Using multiple speakers or synthesized speech would have reduced this potential confound.
issues.quote: The nonwords were pronounced by an adult female native speaker of British English and recorded in stereo at a sampling rate of 22,050 Hz. Items were presented to her in the IPA transcription format
